planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; wintersweet is slow to establish and slow to reach flowering size from seed, so container stock is the standard way to plant it.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade against a warm wall or in a sheltered spot near a path where its fragrance can be appreciated up close; wintersweet is an old Chinese garden shrub grown for one thing above all — intensely sweet, spicy fragrance from small, waxy, translucent pale-yellow flowers with maroon-purple centers that open on bare gray branches in the dead of winter, often during a warm spell between freezes, well before the glossy leaves emerge. A single stem cut and brought indoors will scent an entire room. The shrub itself is an unremarkable, rangy, multi-stemmed grower with plain foliage the rest of the year, so site it where winter interest matters and something else can carry the summer show, such as near an entry or a frequently used winter path. It tolerates partial shade but flowers most heavily with several hours of sun. Prune immediately after flowering, since next winter's buds form on the current year's growth; older plants can be renovated by cutting the oldest stems to the ground.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; glossy sarcandra is a slow-growing East Asian forest understory shrub best purchased as an established plant rather than raised from seed.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath established trees or against a shaded wall; glossy sarcandra is an evergreen East Asian understory shrub grown for its glossy, deep-green, sharply toothed foliage and, most of all, for the clusters of small, bright orange-red berries that ripen in late fall and persist through winter, giving deep shade a spot of color when little else is blooming there. The tiny greenish flowers themselves are inconspicuous. Long used in traditional East Asian herbal medicine and prized in Japanese and Chinese flower arranging (ikebana) for its cut branches of glossy leaves and berries, it is grown ornamentally in the West mainly as an unusual, refined evergreen for the woodland shade garden. Keep soil consistently moist and mulch with leaf litter to mimic its native forest floor conditions; protect from hard freezes in the colder end of its hardiness range.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in spring into sandy, well-drained, slightly saline-tolerant soil in partial shade to full sun; boufu grows naturally on Japanese and Okinawan coastal dunes and bluffs and tolerates poor, sandy soil and salt spray better than most culinary herbs.

directions: Direct sow into sandy, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; boufu is a coastal Japanese and Okinawan perennial in the carrot family, grown for its tender young shoots and finely divided, aromatic leaves, which are harvested in spring and used in Okinawan cooking much like a cross between celery and parsley — lightly blanched, added to tempura, or used fresh in salads. It forms a low mound of blue-green, feathery foliage and produces flat clusters of small white flowers on taller stalks if allowed to bolt in its second year. In its native coastal habitat it tolerates sandy soil, salt spray, and part shade from adjacent dune vegetation, making it a good choice for a lean, well-drained herb bed that doesn't stay wet. Harvest young leaves and shoots regularly to keep the plant productive and delay flowering, which coarsens the texture.

planting.note: Direct sow or press small starter plants into crevices in spring in average to poor, well-drained soil in partial shade; Kenilworth ivy readily self-sows once established, tucking its own seed pods into nearby cracks and crevices, so a single planting often spreads on its own without further help.

directions: Plant or sow into average to poor, well-drained soil in partial shade, tucking seed or small starts directly into the crevices of a shaded stone wall, retaining wall, or old masonry steps where it will look most at home; Kenilworth ivy is a delicate, trailing perennial with small, ivy-shaped leaves and tiny snapdragon-like lavender flowers with a yellow throat, blooming from spring through fall. After each flower fades, the seed stalk curves and grows away from the light, pushing the ripening seed pod deep into a dark crevice to germinate there — an adaptation that lets the plant colonize vertical stone and brickwork on its own over time. It is a classic self-seeding plant for softening the look of old shaded walls, steps, and rockeries, and tolerates poor, dry, alkaline soil that would stress most other groundcovers. It can naturalize enthusiastically in the right conditions, so it is best given a spot, like a stone wall, where its spread is welcome rather than a small formal bed.

planting.note: Set out small starter plugs or divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Irish moss knits together into a solid moss-like mat over one growing season with consistent moisture, and struggles badly through hot, humid summers, so afternoon shade is important south of its cool-summer comfort zone.

directions: Plant small starter plugs in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; despite the common name, Irish moss is not a true moss but a mat-forming flowering perennial with tiny, bright-green, needle-like foliage that looks and feels remarkably moss-like underfoot, studded with small white star-shaped flowers in early summer. It is a favorite lawn substitute and filler between flagstones and pavers in cool, mild-summer climates, tolerating light foot traffic once the mat is established. It needs consistently moist soil and struggles in hot, humid, or drought-prone conditions — it thrives in the Pacific Northwest and similar cool-summer regions but performs poorly and often dies out over a hot, humid Gulf South summer, so treat it as a plant for a small, easily watered, part-shade nook rather than a large sunny expanse in warm climates. Water regularly during dry spells and avoid walking on it while newly planted.
